A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the H3O moiety can be considered a precursor of the proton-electron pair.

the H(3)+ radical is not a stable species, and it is only kinetically stabilized by the solvent, which is capable to shift the electron density from the hydrogen end of H(3)+ to its oxygen end, thus forming a solvent-separated pair.
a localized H3 radical can only be stabilized by microsolvation with a large number of water molecules, whereas a localized H3+ radical can be stabilized by a single water.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a single water molecule is not sufficient to stabilize the electronic structure and the reactivity of a localized radical.
a single water molecule is not capable of fully solvating a radical and that the solvated radical is best described as an ion pair.
the H3O radical is a highly reactive species, which is only stable in the gas phase, and that its reactivity is already strongly affected by a single water solvent shell.
